blocks.text: Thirty years ago, Vietnam was far behind Indonesia. In 1994, the income per capita of Indonesia was about US $1,800, while Vietnam was only US $860, less than half. But after three decades, that gap narrows things down. Indonesia is in US $4,370, Vietnam US $4,020. All that's left is one hair. In a year's time in two years, Vietnam will overtake Indonesia.

If you look at the distribution of well-being, the picture is clearer. With international poverty standards US $4.2 per day, by 2023 about 21.9% of Indonesian residents are poor, while Vietnam is only 4.2%. If the enclosure is raised to US $8.3, about 70% of Indonesia is considered poor, Vietnam is about 22%. The difference is not just numbers, but portraits of social-economic imbalance are much sharper in Indonesia.

What's interesting is the development of a new modern Vietnamese economy really took shape since the early 19900s, after they got out of the big war, internal conflict and long social injuries. The economic reform was indeed announced 1986, but real acceleration only occurs when policy direction is made clear and priority narrowed down: growing or drowning. Vietnam lives on a deadline. Indonesia often lives by the assumption that time is always available.
This is the first fundamental difference: crisis as compass
Vietnam grew not because it was comfortable, but because it felt pressured. Crisis forces discipline, focus, and consistency. Policies are not presentation material, but life-or-death decisions.

Indonesia has also experienced a huge crisis of 1997, which unfolds how fragile the economic foundation is, how low the quality of SDM is, and how expensive the political costs that are loaded with KKN and power. But once the fire wears off, we're back in the old cycle. Recycling. Change the bag, fill it is the same The system's a little different, the people are the same. Indonesia is improving on the surface, but fragile at the bottom.

Vietnam treats crisis like a fire alarm; moves to save lives. Indonesia often treats her like an ambulance siren that sounds noisy for a minute and then disappears around the bend. And we're back to making peace with traffic, mental, minor, and KKN alike. The reformation era was just an ambulance siren.
The second difference lies in the growth machine.

Vietnam chooses a simple path but focus: manufacturing and export. They built industrial areas, attracted foreign investments, and accelerated international trade integration. The result was seen from economic structure: Vietnam went up from about 19% of GDP (1988) to about 184% (2022). Vietnam doesn't just trade, they have to trade. And because it has to, discipline turns into culture.

Indonesia is moving in different directions. The symptoms of deindustrialization are getting clearer. The manufacturing ports are down, the formal job opportunities are shrinking, and industrial investors tend to choose a more consistent and more regulated country, with Vietnam becoming one of the main choices. Indonesia is increasingly dependent on commodities of natural resources that are at a cost of fluctuative, unsustainable and failing to push for national productivity. The dependence on global waves makes us go up during high waves, but not able to swim when it goes down.
The third difference is the coherence of policy.

Vietnam is a relative to one command. Decentralization is the achievement of democracy the Reformation Era, but without strong coordination, it turns into a maze of economic cost. Periodization, interpretation of rules, land, layout, retribution, to domestic logistics can all slow down and block investments. Not impossible to overcome, but too expensive and too slow.
We often judge development by procedure, not results. This development by process makes regulation and bureaucracy look like achievement, even though implementation is far from completed.

Vietnam certainly has problems of its own. But they keep the policy straight: pull investment, build manufacturing bases, push exports, cut obstacles. The consistency is not a coincidence. That's the result of a crisis.
What lesson can we take? Four unpostponed priorities.
First, return the manufacturing industry to the construction stage

In the last three decades, Indonesia has shifted from industry-based economies to service-based economies. Our industrial labor share is stagnant, about 22%. That number also helps to be loved by mines, not manufacturing. While Vietnam absorbs 31% of its labor in industry, most of its manufacturing. As a result, millions of Indonesian workers are educated low and middle-class forced to enter the service sector and informal wage.

Indonesian poverty rate that is 70% with international standards $8.3 a day is not just statistics. It's proof that without a strong manufacturing industry engine, the majority of labor forces are hard to develop. To cut poverty and expand the productive job opportunity, the manufacturing industry must be an economic locomotive, while transitioning to industry and service-tech prepared.
Second, tidying up coordination and confirming rules so that the investment climate doesn't get choked up.

Indonesia is not a lack of regulation, we're just overdoing it. What is lacking is consistency and certainty. Cross-sector and area coordination is often out of tune, different permits interpretation, and long administrative processes. For investors, what's expensive is not official costs, it's uncertainty.

This is what makes a lot of foreign companies choose their neighbors. Indonesia needs to leave a developmental mindset by projectile, as if to make the same rules as building. All we need is development by execution: simple, clear rules, and enforced without compromise.
Third, build export discipline: logistics efficient, labor productivity, and consistent quality standards

East Asia countries like Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China and Malaysia grow through exports of displines. They use global markets to test the quality of their industry. Vietnam does the same thing: fixing logistics, building industrial zones, strengthening vocation education, and keeping policy affirmation.

Indonesia doesn't have that discipline yet. High logistics costs, standard products are not uniform, and productivity is left behind. If manufacturing is going to rise, exports should be the main stage. Without export orientation, the national industry will continue to spin in small pools while other countries swim in the ocean.
Fourth, the transformation of national innovation ecosystem: higher education, R & D, and SDM development

This is the foundation of a global economy that has been less touched. Our higher education system hasn't been designed to produce global grade SDM. The R & D national is still very low in funding, capacity, and relevance to industry. College is often stuck as a "hate factory," not a research and innovation center. As a result, the industry is poor productivity and the country is poor innovation.

Vietnam has set up its inovation ecosystem a decade ago. Indonesia is still busy with internal issues, administrative procedures, and campus political dynamics. Without the transformation of the ecosystem, innovation, high-end education, relevant research, superior HR, and priority industry, we will continue to be trapped in a middle income trap.

I tried to voice this need through the book NOW or NEVER, which outlined the blueprint of the transformative ecosystem of national innovation. However, in the homeland, public conversations are often dragged by gossip, social media, and jargon. Critical thinking requires common sense and attention; two things that are unfortunately very rare. We have a very short ratio, and only about 1% of the population is actually capable of critical thinking deeply.
At the end of the day, the whole point of our problem is the midset.
Vietnam ran because they felt little time. There's a sense of crisis that leads to a decision.

Indonesia is taking it easy because it feels like time is high. It's like there's no deadline. The blunt crisis makes innovative solutions common, when the challenges we face are chronic. History repeats: a nation that thinks time is an ally, often runs out of time.

If Indonesia wants to really move forward, we have to grow sense of crisis and sense of urgency. This was before the distance with Vietnam dilated not just a hair, but it turned into a new abyss. Just like our gaping distance with China today, which is also behind us three decades ago: they went from income per capita to US $1,400, when Indonesia was already at US $1,800.

(Elwin Tobing, Economic Professor, the President of INADATA, Irvine, U.S.; Writing Book AWW or NEVER that gives blueprint the transformation of the national ecosystem of innovation as a absolute requirement to 2050 Gold Indonesia.
